---
name: plan-first
description: >-
  Front door for work that will span more than one file, review unit, or
  commit. Produces the plan before the first edit: the claim, the done-gate,
  the slice boundaries, the gates that will run, and the base it runs against.
  Names the invariants that apply rather than restating them. Use before
  authoring implementation work, or when a task is about to become a PR stack.
---

# Plan first

Most rework is a constraint discovered late that was knowable early. This
produces the plan while changing the plan is still free.

It carries **no invariants of its own**. Invariants live in `principle-*`
skills, which is why they survive a plan being wrong. This file names them and
stops.

## When this is worth it

Run it when the work will cross a file, a review unit, or a commit. Skip it
for a one-file change with a local check — planning a two-line fix costs more
than the fix.

The tell that it was skipped: a gate rejects the shape of the work rather than
its content ("mixed review units", "changed without a corresponding test
change"). That is a planning failure surfacing as a build failure.

## Step 0. Scan the past decisions on the code you will touch

Before the claim, read what earlier changes to this area decided. For each
file or guard the plan changes:

```sh
git log --oneline -15 -- <file>
gh pr view <number> --json title,body
git log -S '<token>' --oneline
```

The first lists the PR numbers of recent decisions, the second reads the ones
that set the current shape, and the third finds who added the check or rule
you will change.

For a small area, run these inline. For more than a couple of files, or
any plan that removes, reverses, or loosens something, hand this to the
`why` skill's decision-history investigator (a read-only helper agent)
here, not after the diff exists. Record what you found on the `History:` line of the output.

## Step 1. State the claim and the done-gate

One sentence each:

- **Claim** — the single thing a reviewer is being asked to approve.
- **Done-gate** — the command or artifact that passes when the claim holds.

If the done-gate is not a command, say what you will show instead. "It works"
is not a done-gate; `principle-prove-it` will reject it later, so reject it
now while it costs nothing.

Two claims means two slices. Go to Step 2.

## Step 2. Derive the slices before writing any of them

Delegate to `split-scope`. Decide the boundaries from what the repo's own
review units are, not from what is convenient to write.

Name, per slice: the claim, the review unit, and why it cannot merge with its
neighbour. A slice that needs a sibling's file to pass its own gates is not a
slice — it is one slice pretending to be two.

Order them so evidence precedes the change it justifies: a repro before its
fix, a rule before the gate that enforces it, a foundation before the
behavior on top.

## Step 3. List the gates now, at the scope they will run

This is the step that pays for the whole playbook.

Find the repo's gate runner (a preflight script, a CI workflow, a documented
check list) and write down which gates each slice will trip. Then check each
one's **scope**: a gate invoked with a wider default than the slice can report
clean on work it never compared.

A gate you discover at publish time is a re-split. A gate whose scope you
never checked is a false pass.

## Step 4. Pin the base

Name the ref every slice is planned against, and confirm it is current. For a
stack, that base moves: if the bottom merges while the top is in flight, and
the merge was a squash, the upper slices still carry commits that are no
longer ancestors, and every one of them conflicts.

Decide now whether the stack tolerates the base moving, or whether it must
land as a unit.

## Step 5. Name the invariants, do not restate them

List the `principle-*` skills this work triggers, each with the decision it
changes. A principle named with no decision behind it was name-dropped.

If a principle would forbid the plan, the plan changes here — not after the
diff exists.

## Step 6. Pick the products, then stop planning

Name which procedures run and in what order — `how` and `why` before editing
unfamiliar code (Step 0 already ran the history part of `why`), `alternatives-considered` plus `spike-and-validate` for a
decision expensive to reverse, the repo's verification and PR skills at the
end.

Then stop. A plan that keeps growing is avoiding the work.

## Output

```text
History:   <PRs read> — <decision each one made that this plan keeps or changes>
Claim:      <one sentence>
Done-gate:  <command, or what you will show>
Slices:     <n>  — <unit> · <claim> · <why separate>
Gates:      <gate> at <scope>
Base:       <ref> — current as of <check>
Invariants: <principle-name> → <decision it changed>
Products:   <ordered list>
Unknowns:   <what would change the plan if it turns out otherwise>
```

`Unknowns` is not optional. A plan with no unknowns has not been examined.

## Do not

- Restate an invariant's content here. Name it and link it.
- Plan a one-file change with a local check.
- Keep planning after Step 6.
- Treat a gate's default scope as the slice's scope.
# What must be replaced to port `jev-pokemon` from Red to Emerald

## Decision

Forking `christianmat/jev-pokemon` is a good way to preserve its JEV policy
protocol, logging, and control-loop shape. It is **not** a ROM swap or a
small emulator adapter change. The original harness has Pokémon Red / Game
Boy assumptions throughout its emulator, RAM decoder, ROM parser, text/menu
reader, pathfinder, battle facts, and milestones.

The safe boundary remains:

```text
mGBA raw bytes + frames + GBA keys
  -> Emerald ROM-profile decoder
  -> typed, stable GameState
  -> branch classifier + finite LegalAction[]
  -> JEV selected action ID
  -> validated GBA input sequence
  -> observed outcome / replay log
```

JEV must receive neither raw addresses nor raw key presses.

## Emulator choice: mGBA vs PyBoyAdvance

**Decision boundary:** this selection fixes the `EmulatorAdapter` process
topology, checkpoint strategy, and test/replay model. It is expensive to
reverse after the state decoder and executor depend on an API.

| Option | Status | Bridge difficulty | Emulator / delivery risk | Recommendation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **mGBA + Lua + local controller** | **Considered:** mGBA documents memory/bus reads, key masks, frame stepping, callbacks, screenshots, and save states; it ships a Gen-3 Pokémon demo with an Emerald US profile. | Higher initial integration cost: define a small request/response transport and keep Lua polling/stepping while the controller awaits JEV. | Lower: mature GBA emulator surface, explicit save-state support, and a pre-existing Emerald decoding reference. | **Default for the durable harness.** |
| **PyBoyAdvance in-process Python** | **Considered:** inspected at commit `f2ff0ec6657964b9fffdbbdeeecee7043385c2a8`. | Lower prototype cost: Python directly exposes `frame`, 10-button press/release, RGB frame buffer, and bus memory. No Lua or IPC layer. | Higher: the project labels itself experimental, says games may not work, requires a BIOS, has no emulator snapshot/load API in the inspected source, and has no Emerald-specific test. | Use only behind the same `EmulatorAdapter` interface, after the spike below passes. Do not select it because its API feels simpler. |

PyBoyAdvance therefore reduces **bridge code** but can increase **whole-project
risk**. It is a credible prototype option, not evidence that Emerald runs
correctly enough for replayable automation. Its low-level memory methods also
permit writes; the adapter must expose only read telemetry and normal key
input regardless of the emulator chosen.

### PyBoyAdvance qualification spike

Before making PyBoyAdvance the emulator decision, run this small disposable
experiment on the exact legally obtained Emerald ROM/BIOs and keep only its
results:

1. Boot to title screen, begin a new game, and reach Birch's starter decision.
2. Drive that path only through `press_key`/`release_key` plus deterministic
   `frame` calls; compare stable screenshots and selected RAM invariants.
3. Create the game's Flash 1M save, launch a new process, reload it, and prove
   the same state is recovered. Also prove a checkpoint/rollback mechanism;
   PyBoyAdvance exposes backup save writing but no emulator save-state/load
   API was found in the inspected source.
4. Select a starter, finish the first forced battle, and compare party, HP,
   flags, and replay timing across several clean runs.

Failure of any step keeps mGBA as the selected backend. Success makes
PyBoyAdvance a supported backend candidate, but does not remove the
Emerald-specific decoder/menu/battle work described below.

## Reuse with little or no semantic change

| Original area | Why it survives | Required adaptation |
|---|---|---|
| `src/jev/types.ts` | It defines a generic JSON request: state plus choice/score/boolean questions, and a typed answer. | Rename only if desired; retain option IDs as the action boundary. |
| `src/jev/client.ts` | Caching, throttling, retries, call logs, and probability sampling do not depend on Pokémon generation. | Make idle-frame ticking call the new mGBA adapter. |
| `src/jev/gateway.ts` | It serializes the generic typed request to JEV. | Retain; test against recorded responses. |
| Logging/checkpoint/replay idea | Decision record, state fingerprint, legal actions, compiled input, and observed result remain valuable. | Define a versioned Emerald record schema. |
| Agent dispatch pattern | The small `observe/classify -> choose -> execute` loop is the right decomposition. | Rebuild the Red-specific tracking and mode predicates it calls. |

## Replace outright

| Original area | Red-specific assumption | Emerald replacement |
|---|---|---|
| `src/emu/emulator.ts` | In-process `serverboy` Game Boy core, direct JavaScript memory array, 8 buttons. | mGBA Lua bridge + local controller protocol. Expose GBA key masks, frame stepping, state files, and a deliberately read-only telemetry API. |
| `src/game/symbols.ts` | Generated `pokered` symbols and fixed locations. | `EmeraldRomProfile`: ROM SHA-256, known globals, struct offsets, text/table metadata, and startup invariants. |
| `src/game/state.ts` | Red WRAM field names, 44-byte Gen-1 party entries, fixed tile map and menu registers. | Decoder for Emerald runtime state, SaveBlock pointers, Gen-3 Pokémon structures, battle controller state, menu/text/cursor state, scripts and input lock. |
| `src/game/rom.ts` | Red ROM banks, map headers, type chart, species/move/item tables and object encodings. | Emerald data reader, preferably derived from an exact profile / decomp symbols for a validated target build. |
| `src/game/text.ts` and menu decoding | Red font, 20×18 tile map and cursor glyph conventions. | Emerald character map and UI-specific readers. Use RAM telemetry first; use screenshots only to corroborate visible prompts. |
| `src/game/world.ts`, `regions.ts` | Red collision and map graph formats. | Emerald map-group/event/connection/object/collision model, with dynamic scripts and avatar readiness. |
| `src/agent/battle.ts` | Gen-1 damage, catch, physical/special, Safari, and menu mechanics. | Emerald legal-action builder. It must support Gen-3 mechanics and branch explicitly for singles, doubles, targets, forced switches, item restrictions and special battles. |
| `src/knowledge/milestones.ts` | Red event flags and story locations. | Emerald goals and validated event-flag predicates. |
| `src/agent/{battle,dialog,menus,field,overworld}.ts` and `context.ts` | These contain Red mechanics, UI labels, badge bits, symbols, movement and 44-byte-mon assumptions—not just generic orchestration. | Audit each module; preserve only abstractions that survive a concrete Emerald contract test. |

## Adapt cautiously

| Area | What changes |
|---|---|
| Mode classifier | Preserve the idea of `boot`, `busy`, `overworld`, `dialog/menu`, and `battle`, but base it on Emerald callbacks/tasks/scripts, input lock, menu state and battle controller requests—not only an in-battle byte. |
| Overworld decisions | Retain semantic candidate selection, but rebuild candidate generation and path execution around Emerald maps and runtime objects. Scripts may ignore keys or move the avatar. |
| Menu executor | Retain cursor-relative execution and postcondition checks. Re-measure all frame holds/releases; never assume Red timings or menu layout. |
| Battle facts | Continue giving JEV legal moves and explanatory facts. Calculate only facts whose Emerald mechanic has been implemented and tested; unknown legality is a reason to withhold an action, not guess. |
| Save states | Retain checkpoint/retry concept but treat mGBA states as opaque, versioned emulator artifacts. Keep ROMs and saves user-local. |

## Emerald-specific risks that invalidate a “small adaptation” estimate

1. **The hardware/emulator boundary changes.** mGBA Lua provides raw reads
   *and writes*, key masks, frame control, callbacks, screenshots and save
   states; it does not provide Pokémon state or a JEV integration. The new
   bridge must intentionally expose only reads plus normal controller input,
   and its local controller protocol is new production code.
2. **Addresses require a profile.** Emerald's SaveBlocks are pointer-based and
   relocated. A decoder must locate profile-known pointer globals before it
   reads struct offsets; hard-coding a single observed EWRAM address is unsafe.
3. **Gen-3 Pokémon data is harder.** Persistent Pokémon use encrypted,
   personality-selected substructures. Party and battle copies are related but
   not interchangeable.
4. **A frame is not a choice boundary.** Text printing, animation, scripts,
   map loads and battle-controller sequences span variable frames. The bridge
   needs readiness predicates and action verifiers.
5. **Battle legality is broader.** Full general play must handle doubles,
   target selection, forced replacements, trapping, item restrictions,
   special encounters and UI branches. An MVP may declare most of these
   unsupported, but must detect and safely stop/reject such modes rather than
   treat a single-battle menu as universal.
6. **World routing is a new parser.** Emerald map groups, events, dynamic
   objects and scripts make Red's region graph non-portable.
7. **Python-native does not remove the game adapter.** PyBoyAdvance can expose
   direct Python frame/input/screen/memory access, but it supplies no Pokémon
   semantics. Its README explicitly calls it experimental and notes that some
   games may not function, so compatibility and save/replay behavior are
   additional qualification work rather than a shortcut.

## Minimal proof that proves the architecture

Target one checksum-verified US Emerald v1.0 ROM profile and a user-local
checkpoint at Professor Birch's starter decision.

1. Lua bridge proves mGBA capabilities at startup and serves requests from a
   local controller without blocking frame callbacks.
2. Decoder recognizes the starter prompt, three legal starter options, and
   current cursor.
3. JEV receives only those three semantic options and selects one.
4. Executor moves from the observed cursor, presses GBA keys, and verifies the
   selected starter entered the party.
5. Decoder recognizes the first forced battle and emits only legal move actions.
6. Executor verifies battle victory, writing a replayable record for each
   decision.

This slice establishes the bridge, profile, typed policy, input compiler, and
verifier. It does **not** establish full overworld routing, general menus, or
the complete Gen-3 battle matrix.

### Delivery order

1. **Transport + decoder parity:** establish non-blocking Lua/controller IPC
   and validate party/count/species reads against mGBA's shipped Gen-3 Pokémon
   demo. That demo already has an Emerald US profile, but is only a reference
   decoder—not a world, menu, battle, or JEV harness.
2. **Deterministic replay:** drive one known menu from a state checkpoint with
   no JEV call; assert the exact typed observation and input postcondition.
3. **JEV vertical slice:** add the three starter options, first forced-battle
   legal-move branch, recorded responses, and victory verification.

## Gates before expanding scope

- Reject ROM hashes not explicitly profiled. Compute SHA-256 in the controller
  (or use mGBA's exposed CRC32/SHA-1 checks); do not imply Lua natively offers
  SHA-256.
- Assert pointer ranges and decoded-state invariants before every decision.
- Never write game RAM in the harness; use only normal controller input.
- Ask JEV only at a stable, classified decision boundary.
- Reject a JEV answer not present in the current legal action set.
- Use battle structures for battle facts; a persistent encrypted `Pokemon`
  and runtime `BattlePokemon` are distinct representations.
- Verify each action's expected postcondition before the next decision.
- Record enough data to replay failures without calling JEV again.

## Sources

- `https://github.com/christianmat/jev-pokemon` at commit
  `dd8b18cd97923cdfc547e9c1acecfe4fb831c442`: emulator wrapper,
  Red state/ROM readers, agent loop, and JEV types/client.
- `https://mgba.io/docs/scripting.html`: Lua scripting API.
- `https://github.com/mgba-emu/mgba` at commit
  `1d201b22a86d31dfb3bc75145403711f6762015f`: scripting implementation and
  Gen-3 Pokémon Lua demo, including its Emerald US profile.
- `https://github.com/williamckha/PyBoyAdvance` at commit
  `f2ff0ec6657964b9fffdbbdeeecee7043385c2a8`: Python-native GBA emulator;
  its README marks it experimental and its source was inspected for frame,
  input, memory, screen, persistence, and state APIs.
- `EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_PLAN.md`: local proposed v1 architecture; it is not an
  implementation.

    16	<div class="eyebrow">Architecture research · 26 September 2026</div>
    17	<h1>Pokémon Emerald × JEV</h1>
    18	<p class="lede">What must change to move the <em>Jev Plays Pokémon Red</em> harness onto Emerald with mGBA—and, crucially, what should not change.</p>
    19	<p class="verdict">The JEV request/choice protocol is reusable. The substantial work is building the Emerald-specific boundary that turns mGBA’s raw bytes and key masks into safe, typed decisions.</p>
    20	<ul class="toc"><li><a href="#core">Core diagram</a></li><li><a href="#states">State layers</a></li><li><a href="#decision">How JEV decides</a></li><li><a href="#port">Port complexity</a></li><li><a href="#emulator">Emulator choice</a></li><li><a href="#sources">Evidence</a></li></ul>
    21	</header>
    22	
    23	<section id="core">
    24	<h2>The core: five boundaries, one narrow decision choke point</h2>
    25	<div class="diagram"><div class="flow">
    26	<div class="node raw"><h3>1. mGBA + Lua</h3><span class="tag">raw machine state</span><ul><li>bus / memory-domain reads</li><li>frame count and callback timing</li><li>GBA 10-key bitmask</li><li>save/load state; screenshot</li></ul><p class="small">No Pokémon concepts here.</p></div><div class="arrow">→</div>
    27	<div class="node typed"><h3>2. Emerald profile decoder</h3><span class="tag">typed game state</span><ul><li>read ROM-profile globals and dereference SaveBlock pointers</li><li>decode party, bag, flags, map, objects, battle, menu, text</li><li>recognize stable / input-ready boundaries</li></ul><p class="small">Owns version-specific addresses, text encoding and layouts.</p></div><div class="arrow">→</div>
    28	<div class="node branch"><h3>3. Classifier + legal branch</h3><span class="tag">decision state</span><ul><li>classify: battle / dialog / menu / overworld / busy</li><li>construct only currently legal semantic actions</li><li>attach facts: PP, type effect, route distance, risk</li></ul><p class="small">This is the protective adapter around JEV.</p></div><div class="arrow">→</div>
    29	<div class="node policy"><h3>4. JEV policy</h3><span class="tag">typed choice</span><ul><li>input: <code>{ state, questions }</code></li><li>question: <code>choice</code>, <code>score</code>, or <code>boolean</code></li><li>output: option ID, optionally probabilities</li></ul><p class="small">It ranks the supplied alternatives; it does not manipulate RAM or press buttons.</p></div><div class="arrow">→</div>
    30	<div class="node execute"><h3>5. Executor + verifier</h3><span class="tag">controller effect</span><ul><li>validate selected ID</li><li>compile intent into cursor-relative buttons and frame holds</li><li>observe expected outcome; log / checkpoint / safely retry</li></ul><p class="small">The game sees only normal controller input.</p></div><div class="arrow">↺</div>
    31	<div class="node raw"><h3>Next observation</h3><span class="tag">evidence</span><ul><li>did selection move?</li><li>did text / battle phase advance?</li><li>did map, flag, HP, menu or party change?</li></ul><p class="small">Feeds the next stable decision point.</p></div>
    32	</div></div>
    33	<p class="callout"><strong>Do not wire JEV directly to mGBA.</strong> Raw addresses are ROM-version details; raw button sequences are timing-sensitive. The bridge should accept only a validated semantic action (for example, <code>use_move:2</code>) and be solely responsible for the button choreography.</p>
    34	</section>
    35	
    36	<section id="states">
    37	<h2>“Each possible state” — the useful answer is layered</h2>
    38	<p>A complete enumeration of Pokémon’s machine states is astronomically large. The harness instead gives each layer a different, finite job. “Possible” below means the state families the bridge must represent, not every numeric value or every story permutation.</p>
    39	<table><thead><tr><th>Layer</th><th>Possible states / contents</th><th>Who creates it</th><th>What JEV receives?</th></tr></thead><tbody>
    40	<tr><td><strong>Emulator snapshot</strong></td><td>GBA CPU/registers; ROM; BIOS; EWRAM, IWRAM, MMIO, VRAM, palette and OAM; framebuffer; current frame; key mask; full save state.</td><td>mGBA</td><td class="no">No</td></tr>
    41	<tr><td><strong>Emerald decoded state</strong></td><td>ROM profile identity; pointers and SaveBlocks; game callback/task/script lock; map group/number, position, facing, motion; object events; party/PC/bag/money; flags/vars; dialog/menu/cursor; battle participants, status, PP, side conditions, phase and legal UI state.</td><td>Profile decoder</td><td>Usually no—only a projection</td></tr>
    42	<tr><td><strong>Harness mode</strong></td><td><code>boot</code>, <code>busy</code>, <code>overworld</code>, <code>dialog/menu</code>, <code>battle</code>. A state can be observable yet <em>not decision-ready</em>.</td><td>Situation classifier</td><td>Only decision-ready modes</td></tr>
    43	<tr><td><strong>Decision branch</strong></td><td>One current branch plus a finite action set. Examples: starter choice; YES/NO; menu row; route target; battle action; move; target; party switch; item target; nickname character.</td><td>Legal-action generator</td><td class="yes">Yes</td></tr>
    44	<tr><td><strong>Harness memory</strong></td><td>Goal/milestone, visited maps, recent dialog/actions, failed choices, blocked exits, chosen focus, checkpoint/replay history.</td><td>Controller process</td><td class="yes">Compact projection</td></tr>
    45	</tbody></table>
    46	<div class="two"><div class="card"><h3>Red harness’s actual mode classifier</h3><p>It recognizes five modes: <code>battle</code>, <code>dialog</code>, <code>overworld</code>, <code>busy</code>, and <code>boot</code>. “Busy” means wait rather than call JEV—important because cutscenes and transitions can ignore input.</p></div><div class="card"><h3>Emerald’s essential extra distinction</h3><p>In Emerald, <code>inBattle</code> alone is insufficient. Battle controller buffers and execution flags can mean animation or a selection protocol is still in progress. Prompt only when the player can actually make the relevant choice.</p></div></div>
    47	</section>
    48	
    49	<section id="decision">
    50	<h2>How state gets into JEV, and how the decision is made</h2>
    51	<div class="two"><div class="card"><h3>What crosses the boundary</h3><p>The JEV client sends structured JSON:</p><pre><code>{
    52	  state: { objective, party, bag, location, recentDialog,
    53	           battle: { enemy, active, ... } },
    54	  questions: {
    55	    decision: { type: "choice", instructions: "...",
    56	                criteria: { "Use Ember": "Fire; 25 PP; ...",
    57	                            "Switch to X": "..." } }
    58	  }
    59	}</code></pre><p>The model returns a selected key (and may return probabilities). It does not get arbitrary RAM, symbols, coordinates to invent, or a button API.</p></div><div class="card"><h3>What “JEV decides” actually means</h3><p>JEV chooses the best <em>supplied</em> option based on the typed state and option descriptions. The real JEV model’s internal scoring is external and not exposed by this repository.</p><p>The harness decision logic remains very substantial: it computes legal options and facts, filters impossible actions, caches/throttles calls, detects lack of progress, may sample from model probabilities to escape loops, and can restore a checkpoint as a last resort.</p></div></div>
    60	<h3>Decision surfaces to port</h3>
    61	<table><thead><tr><th>Situation</th><th>Semantic choices JEV may receive</th><th>Harness-provided facts / mechanics</th></tr></thead><tbody>
    62	<tr><td>Overworld</td><td>Focus: progress, heal, train, catch, shop, explore, team; then reachable warp/exit/NPC/sign/grass/item/field-move target.</td><td>Collision and route graph, A* path, objective distance, availability, visited/blocked history.</td></tr>
    63	<tr><td>Dialog & menus</td><td>Visible menu rows, YES/NO, name characters, cancel/continue, party/item choices.</td><td>Decoded text/cursor, row labels, cursor movement and confirm/back button sequence.</td></tr>
    64	<tr><td>Normal battle</td><td>Fight → legal move/target; bag → legal item/target; switch → legal party member; run where allowed.</td><td>PP, disabled/trapped states, targets, type effectiveness, damage/catch estimates, HP/status, battle-specific prohibitions.</td></tr>
    65	<tr><td>Special battle</td><td>Safari, double battle, forced replacement, tutorial/Wally, capture and other special menus.</td><td>Separate branch schemas; never assume the regular four-action menu is valid.</td></tr>
    66	</tbody></table>
    67	<p class="small">The bundled mock backend is not the real model: it scores positive/negative words in option descriptions, adds noise, softmaxes, then takes the highest score. It is valuable only as a protocol/offline test double.</p>
    68	</section>
    69	
    70	<section id="port">
    71	<h2>How much more complicated is Emerald?</h2>
    72	<p class="small">Local source for the proposed first slice: <code>EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_PLAN.md</code>.</p>
    73	<p><strong>Engineering-surface estimate: roughly 2–4× the Red port, not a simple line-for-line conversion.</strong> This is an informed sizing judgment from the inspected code, not a measured schedule. The typed JEV client stays close to unchanged; the game adapter and semantic extraction grow materially.</p>
    74	<table><thead><tr><th>Area</th><th>Red implementation</th><th>Emerald / mGBA consequence</th><th>Port status</th></tr></thead><tbody>
    75	<tr><td>Emulator control</td><td>In-process Node <code>serverboy</code> wrapper exposes memory, frame and buttons.</td><td>mGBA Lua exposes bus reads, key masks, <code>runFrame</code>, callbacks and states. Build a local Lua ↔ controller IPC protocol; do not block hot callbacks on remote inference.</td><td>Replace</td></tr>
    76	<tr><td>RAM identity</td><td>Fixed Red symbols from generated <code>pokered</code> data.</td><td>Pin an exact ROM hash/profile. Emerald SaveBlock pointers are relocated; read known pointer globals first, then decode offsets. Validate invariants at startup.</td><td>Replace</td></tr>
    77	<tr><td>Pokémon data</td><td>Gen 1 party layout is simple fixed fields.</td><td>Gen 3 Pokémon have encrypted/shuffled substructures keyed by personality and OT ID. mGBA’s own Pokémon Lua demo shows this decoding work.</td><td>Replace</td></tr>
    78	<tr><td>Maps & routing</td><td>Red ROM parser plus collision grid/A* and a region graph.</td><td>Map groups, connections, scripts, dynamic objects, avatar transition states and locked input demand a fresh Emerald map/control model.</td><td>Replace</td></tr>
    79	<tr><td>Battle legality</td><td>Gen 1 mechanics and menu branches.</td><td>Gen 3 requires battle-controller synchronization and supports doubles, targets, abilities/items and special contexts. Start v1 with the forced starter battle.</td><td>Replace incrementally</td></tr>
    80	<tr><td>JEV protocol/client</td><td>Typed request, choice IDs, logging, cache/throttle/retry.</td><td>Same shape. Retain it behind a narrow policy interface.</td><td>Reuse</td></tr>
    81	<tr><td>Intent-to-buttons/verifier</td><td>Cursor helpers, input timing, outcome checks.</td><td>Same architectural role, but remeasure Emerald timings and menu contracts.</td><td>Adapt</td></tr>
    82	</tbody></table>
    83	<h3>Best minimal vertical slice</h3>
    84	<p>Use one checksum-verified US Emerald v1.0 profile and a user-local checkpoint at Birch’s starter decision. Decode only the starter menu and forced first battle; let JEV choose the starter and legal moves; execute through mGBA key masks; verify starter party state and battle victory. This proves every boundary before committing to world routing or the full battle matrix.</p>
    85	<p class="callout"><strong>mGBA bridge contract:</strong> address whether a read is a <em>bus address</em> (<code>emu:read*</code>) or a memory-domain <em>offset</em> (<code>emu.memory.*:read*</code>). Keep v1 telemetry read-only. Treat screenshots as optional corroboration: the Lua API saves a screenshot file, rather than supplying a direct image buffer.</p>
    86	</section>
    87	
    88	<section id="emulator">
    89	<h2>Emulator choice: mGBA vs PyBoyAdvance</h2>
    90	<p class="small">Sources: <a href="https://mgba.io/docs/scripting.html">mGBA scripting API</a>; <a href="https://github.com/williamckha/PyBoyAdvance/tree/f2ff0ec6657964b9fffdbbdeeecee7043385c2a8">PyBoyAdvance commit f2ff0ec</a>.</p>
    91	<p><strong>Recommendation: keep mGBA as the durable backend.</strong> PyBoyAdvance reduces bridge code, but raises emulator-compatibility, persistence, and replay risk. This is a product-risk decision, not a preference for Lua versus Python.</p>
    92	<table><thead><tr><th>Question</th><th>mGBA + Lua bridge</th><th>PyBoyAdvance in-process Python</th></tr></thead><tbody>
    93	<tr><td>Controller integration</td><td>Lua reads memory, sets the GBA key mask, advances frames, and talks to a local controller over a small protocol. This adds IPC/orchestration work.</td><td>Direct Python <code>frame</code>, <code>press_key</code>/<code>release_key</code>, 10 GBA buttons, raw memory object, and RGB NumPy/PIL screen make a quick prototype simpler.</td></tr>
    94	<tr><td>State/checkpoint facilities</td><td>Documented callbacks, screenshots, and save/load state buffers/files/slots.</td><td>Inspected source has backup-save writing, but no emulator snapshot, load-state, rewind, or state-serialization API. Its RAM API is internal and needs an access-type argument.</td></tr>
    95	<tr><td>Emerald evidence</td><td>Ships a Gen-3 Pokémon Lua demo with an Emerald US party profile and encrypted-Pokémon decoder.</td><td>No Pokémon/Emerald test was found. Tests are generic homebrew / framebuffer cases; the repository README labels the emulator experimental and warns that games may not function.</td></tr>
    96	<tr><td>Persistence risk</td><td>Use emulator save states plus user-local battery saves.</td><td>Emerald uses 128 KiB Flash 1M. The source detects <code>FLASH1M_V</code> and implements Flash128, but that work is newer than the inspected v1.0.1 release and has no Emerald coverage.</td></tr>
    97	<tr><td>Overall harness difficulty</td><td><strong>Moderate bridge difficulty; lower emulator risk.</strong> The hard work remains Emerald decoding and legal-action construction.</td><td><strong>High/unknown total risk.</strong> It removes Lua IPC, but adds compatibility qualification, checkpoint/restore implementation, and ownership of a less mature emulator API.</td></tr>
    98	</tbody></table>
    99	<h3>Qualification gate for PyBoyAdvance</h3>
   100	<p>Do not select it on API appearance alone. On the exact owned Emerald ROM and BIOS, require: deterministic title → new-game → starter → first-battle input replay; matching EWRAM/screenshot milestones against an mGBA baseline; a 131,072-byte Flash save that reloads in a fresh process; three matching runs; and a measured frame rate. A boot, battle, save/reload, or replay divergence rejects it as this harness’s backend.</p>
   101	<p class="callout"><strong>Invariant for either emulator:</strong> the adapter—not the emulator—must expose only read telemetry and normal controller input. Both underlying engines can write memory; the JEV boundary must never permit that.</p>
   102	</section>

   105	<h2>Evidence and limits</h2>
   106	<p>Repository claims below were read from the linked source. The local workspace presently contains the design plan, not an executable Emerald bridge; its claims are therefore proposal, not implementation evidence.</p>

What must change to move the Jev Plays Pokémon Red harness onto Emerald with mGBA—and, crucially, what should not change.

EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:19:

The JEV request/choice protocol is reusable. The substantial work is building the Emerald-specific boundary that turns mGBA’s raw bytes and key masks into safe, typed decisions.

EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:26:

1. mGBA + Lua

raw machine state
  • bus / memory-domain reads
  • frame count and callback timing
  • GBA 10-key bitmask
  • save/load state; screenshot

No Pokémon concepts here.

→
EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:33:

Do not wire JEV directly to mGBA. Raw addresses are ROM-version details; raw button sequences are timing-sensitive. The bridge should accept only a validated semantic action (for example, use_move:2) and be solely responsible for the button choreography.

EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:40:Emulator snapshotGBA CPU/registers; ROM; BIOS; EWRAM, IWRAM, MMIO, VRAM, palette and OAM; framebuffer; current frame; key mask; full save state.mGBANo EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:74: EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:75: EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:77: EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:83:

Best minimal vertical slice

EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:84:

Use one checksum-verified US Emerald v1.0 profile and a user-local checkpoint at Birch’s starter decision. Decode only the starter menu and forced first battle; let JEV choose the starter and legal moves; execute through mGBA key masks; verify starter party state and battle victory. This proves every boundary before committing to world routing or the full battle matrix.

EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:85:

mGBA bridge contract: address whether a read is a bus address (emu:read*) or a memory-domain offset (emu.memory.*:read*). Keep v1 telemetry read-only. Treat screenshots as optional corroboration: the Lua API saves a screenshot file, rather than supplying a direct image buffer.

EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:89:

Emulator choice: mGBA vs PyBoyAdvance

EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:90:

Sources: mGBA scripting API; PyBoyAdvance commit f2ff0ec.

EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:91:

Recommendation: keep mGBA as the durable backend. PyBoyAdvance reduces bridge code, but raises emulator-compatibility, persistence, and replay risk. This is a product-risk decision, not a preference for Lua versus Python.

EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:92:
AreaRed implementationEmerald / mGBA consequencePort status
Emulator controlIn-process Node serverboy wrapper exposes memory, frame and buttons.mGBA Lua exposes bus reads, key masks, runFrame, callbacks and states. Build a local Lua ↔ controller IPC protocol; do not block hot callbacks on remote inference.Replace
Pokémon dataGen 1 party layout is simple fixed fields.Gen 3 Pokémon have encrypted/shuffled substructures keyed by personality and OT ID. mGBA’s own Pokémon Lua demo shows this decoding work.Replace
EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:99:

Qualification gate for PyBoyAdvance

EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:100:

Do not select it on API appearance alone. On the exact owned Emerald ROM and BIOS, require: deterministic title → new-game → starter → first-battle input replay; matching EWRAM/screenshot milestones against an mGBA baseline; a 131,072-byte Flash save that reloads in a fresh process; three matching runs; and a measured frame rate. A boot, battle, save/reload, or replay divergence rejects it as this harness’s backend.

EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:112:
  • Official mGBA scripting API — Lua, memory/bus reads, keys, frame stepping, callbacks, screenshots and save states; checked against mGBA scripting implementation.

  • mGBA Pokémon Lua demo — Gen 3 encrypted Pokémon decoding.
    • EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:114:
  • PyBoyAdvance — experimental Python/Cython GBA emulator. Its source was inspected for frame/input/screen/memory/persistence APIs; no Emerald test or emulator-state restore API was found.
    • EMERALD_JEV_HARNESS_ARCHITECTURE.html:117:

+port. Use PyBoyAdvance directly in one Python process and keep the Red project

+to transplant the Red map, RAM, battle, or menu modules.

+|---|---|

+| Cursor-relative D-pad/A executor and a visible/RAM postcondition. | A generic screen OCR system. Use a known checkpoint plus fixed, verified screen/cursor contract first. |
+| Recorded JEV response or a small policy call using the same `{state, questions}` / option-ID contract as Red. | Rewriting the entire TypeScript JEV client in Python. |

+### The smallest useful module boundary

+```text
+prototype.py       owns the frame loop and fixed route to the starter prompt
+pyboy_adapter.py   wraps frame(), keys, screen, and a read-only RAM helper

+   deterministic.
+

+or persist Emerald is a stop signal—not a reason to implement emulator
+features ourselves.
